body:
There are mornings when an army turns a page and believes the chapter is over, while a child outside a capital does not get up and a ship admits a day late that it burned. The thirtieth of September 2026 is such a morning: Baghdad declares four holidays, Hormuz sends a warning late, and the field in the east keeps writing a list that does not keep holidays.

I. The last post

By Wednesday the last American soldiers are to have left the bases in Iraq — Erbil in the north, the edge of Baghdad airport, what still clung to the Green Zone and had, through this year, been quietly moved north before it vanished. It is the second complete departure after 2011, and this time it carries the date of a 2024 agreement that Joe Biden signed and Donald Trump has now finished, even as the same Trump wages war in the Gulf. About two thousand five hundred men stood there in the last years. More than four thousand five hundred Americans have died in this country since 2003, most of them in the years when the first chapter was still called invasion. 1

Prime minister Ali al-Zaidi names the first of October a new day of Iraqi statehood and calls four official holidays, as if sovereignty were a flag hoisted at midnight and then left unwatched. The disarmament of Iran-aligned militias, which was meant to sit beside the withdrawal, has been pushed to the end of June 2027. Ninety days of forbearance against a promise that American strikes will not hit them, then the weapons, sometime, under a state watch that still has to grow. Tehran speaks of a victory for the axis. Iraqi security men speak of room Islamic State could use again.

On Wednesday Iraqi troops drive through Baghdad and through Najaf. Ahmed Salah, seventy, says the departure fills the heart with joy and, in the same breath, asks that the militias give their weapons to the state. The Pentagon declares Inherent Resolve over and speaks of training and intelligence that remain. A yard that is emptied still acquires a master. 16

An army leaves because a calendar says so. The neighbours who stay have no calendar for influence.

II. The fire that arrives late

British maritime watch reports on Tuesday, delayed, what is said to have happened on the evening of the twenty-eighth: a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, hit by a projectile of unclear origin, fire aboard, fire out, crew unhurt, voyage resumed. The warning is called suspicious activity, not an attack, though a projectile struck a ship. Iran had spoken over the weekend of nineteen vessels outside routes Tehran allows. Proof of the nineteen is missing. The one late hit is enough to show the strait is not yet a clause.

Araghchi had expected a formal American reply to the seven-day plan on Tuesday, through Qatar, Oman and Pakistan. On Wednesday Tehran says a U.S. response has arrived. What it contains, no one puts on the table. Expectation becomes an envelope; the envelope does not become an opening. Ship-counters speak of oil moving again toward four fifths of the pre-war flow, by detours, fees and escorts. The rial falls past two and a half million to the dollar. The tap stands. Water beside it finds rills. 7

Whoever thinks a needle is open because barrels arrive somewhere confuses arrival with a treaty. Whoever thinks it closed because a ship burns late confuses a report with a clause. Both hold on the same morning.

III. The child outside the city

Overnight into Tuesday Moscow sends a Zircon or Oniks from Kursk region, two ballistic Iskander or S-400 and one hundred fifty-two drones. Ukraine says all three missiles came down, and one hundred six drones. Impacts remain at twenty-four places. Under the academy wreckage rescuers find a second dead. The count on that house rises to two.

Zelenskyy thanks the United States and Norway for a NASAMS system and a packet of missiles. Early Wednesday a strike in Kyiv region kills a child. Five more people are hurt. The book does not set the child as a punchline. It sets the child because the field has no other honesty than addresses and ages. 12

Taras Vysotskyi says grain prices have risen by a quarter since the Black Sea tightened. The FAO confirms the direction. For countries that must buy wheat, an address in Kyiv region becomes a bill in Africa and Southeast Asia. The field reaches farther than the siren.

IV. The list that knows detours

Since one minute after midnight the northern ban holds, and Tuesday shows who can walk around it. Crown Royal may ship whisky in tanks and finish it beyond the line. Labatt fills some of the beer in American halls. The small still and the brewery without a second address do not have that sentence. A billion dollars on the old count, eighty-seven percent of it drink.

V. At the edge of the page

King Mohammed VI names Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri Morocco’s first woman head of government. That is an office, not yet a thread. Puntland’s sea police free the tanker Honour 25. Five of the crew are dead. In Jalud, in the occupied West Bank, more than a hundred settlers attack a village.

Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv comes down at Tabuk. A cry comes from the cockpit; passengers and two off-duty pilots bring the aircraft down. Both cockpit crew go to hospital. The reports disagree on who held the knife. A thread would be a trial. Today it is a landing. 15 19

The Security Council holds a fourth straw poll on the next secretary-general. The slips stay behind the door. A hall that thinned has not earned a new sentence by that.

The chronicler’s close

The last post in Iraq is a date and a vacuum at once. The field has a child outside Kyiv and a grain bill that runs farther than the siren. The tap has a late flame, an envelope without a clause and a rial that falls. The customs list knows detours for those who keep two addresses.

Open remain Hormuz, the eastern field, the northern list and the empty yard on the Tigris.

Today the book does not leave a finger in an old crack. It lays a leaf on the last post and on the child outside the city and watches what the first of October will make of a holiday and of a siren.
